Graph neural networks (GNNs) represent a molecule or crystal as a graph whose nodes are atoms and whose edges connect neighboring atoms. Interaction (message-passing or convolution) blocks repeatedly update each atom's embedding from its neighbors, using distances and, in some architectures, bond and dihedral angles, and output blocks map the final embeddings to a target such as an energy, force or atomic property. Because the features are learned, GNNs avoid hand-built descriptors, but they still inherit the usual regression problems of data imbalance and limited interpretability. See also [interpretable machine learning](/papers/topics/interpretable-machine-learning/), [imbalanced data](/papers/topics/imbalanced-data/) and [magnetic moments](/papers/topics/magnetic-moments/).

## Embeddings reused for magnetic moment regression (2024)

Sanspeur and Kitchin used GemNet-OC as a per-atom classifier (magnetic or non-magnetic) and then regressed moment magnitudes from its 256-dimensional atom embeddings, reaching a mean absolute error of 0.1 µB. They also found a limitation: because the local convolutions are symmetric, atoms in equivalent environments with opposite spins receive nearly identical embeddings, so the network cannot predict the sign of a moment or the collinear ordering without an explicit spin feature in the input ([Sanspeur 2024](/papers/sanspeur2024/)). Summary: [sanspeur2024](/papers/sanspeur2024/).

## Physics inside a graph network (2024)

The TinNet framework of Huang and coworkers uses a graph convolutional network to predict the parameters of a tight-binding d-band model, keeping the accuracy of a black-box network while producing physically interpretable quantities ([Huang et al. 2024](/papers/huang2024/)). Summary: [huang2024](/papers/huang2024/).

## Atom embeddings as search fingerprints (2022)

Yang, Liu and Kitchin used the last-interaction-block atom embeddings of a modified GemNet-dT, trained on energies, as fingerprints for similarity search in QM9, the Materials Project and OC20. The embeddings encoded element identity and local geometry well enough that queries returned atoms of the same element in similar sites without any explicit element filter, and adsorbed O and acetylene matches in OC20 also had similar projected densities of states. Because the embeddings are learned against energy, molecules they retrieve were far more useful for training a Gaussian process to predict the query energy than Morgan fingerprint neighbors ([Yang et al. 2022](/papers/yang2022a/)). Summary: [yang2022a](/papers/yang2022a/). See also [Similarity search](/papers/topics/similarity-search/).
